title: Counting: COUNT and COUNTA
summary: Learn the difference between counting numbers and counting every non-empty cell, and combine the two in one formula.
intro:
`COUNT` counts only the cells that hold numbers, while `COUNTA` counts every non-empty cell, whether it holds text or a number.

The difference is handy for spotting missing data: the number of names from `COUNTA` minus the number of ages from `COUNT` tells you who did not enter their age as a number.

faq.q: Does `COUNT` count a cell that holds a word?
faq.a: No, `COUNT` counts numbers only. Use `COUNTA` to count text as well.
No, it counts only cells that are not empty.

count-numbers.prompt: This is a workshop sign-up list. `COUNT` counts only the cells that hold numbers. In `B8`, type the formula `=COUNT(B2:B6)` to find how many participants entered their age as a number.

counta-names.prompt: `COUNTA` counts every non-empty cell, text or number. In `B9`, write a formula that counts the participants in the range `A2:A6`.

counta-cities.prompt: How many cities were entered? In `C9`, write a formula that counts the non-empty cells in `C2:C6`.

count-the-gap.prompt: How many participants did not enter their age as a number? In `B10`, write a formula that subtracts the number of ages (`COUNT` on `B2:B6`) from the number of participants (`COUNTA` on `A2:A6`).

text-is-not-counted.prompt: A cell holds the text "twenty". Does `COUNT` count it?
options: Yes, because it is not empty
No, because it does not hold a number
Yes, because the text means a number

count-vs-counta.prompt: What is the difference between `COUNT` and `COUNTA`?
options: `COUNT` counts numbers only, and `COUNTA` counts every non-empty cell
`COUNT` adds the values, and `COUNTA` counts them
